strengths: Novel technical approach combining SAE-driven sparse features with M-orthogonal decomposition for interpretable domain adaptation; Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 provide solid theoretical grounding for closed-form projection and stability

Strong empirical results showing 12-16% relative F1 improvements over baselines across multiple domain partition settings (spatial, temporal, facility-specific) on two large-scale EHR datasets with proper ablations
Comprehensive experimental design including >10 baselines (DANN, RMMD, RSDA, BUA, DAL, RCG, CST, SSRT), oracle/base bounds, and systematic ablation studies demonstrating each component's necessity

Practical interpretability innovation via four-quadrant categorization (label impact × domain sensitivity) that maps sparse dimensions to ICD codes and distinguishes transferable from shift-sensitive evidence

Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation (Appendix I.2), hyperparameters, data splits, comprehensive notation table, and algorithm pseudocode; clinical deployment considerations discussed
Addresses genuine gap in clinical DA—combines robustness (accuracy) with transparency (interpretability), filling important need in healthcare where explainability is prerequisite for adoption
Linear probe analysis (Table 3) provides quantitative evidence of effective feature disentanglement across multiple tasks
weaknesses: Interpretability validation is primarily qualitative—case studies (Figure 2, Appendix J.2-J.4) are illustrative but anecdotal; lacks quantitative metrics, inter-rater reliability studies, or user validation with clinicians to demonstrate explanations are actually useful or trustworthy

Theoretical justification for domain concentration in z relies on informal information-theoretic bounds (≳, ≲ relations) rather than rigorous guarantees; no empirical validation that z independently captures domain information (Table 3 shows 0.09 cosine similarity Wc(v0) vs Wc(z), indicating residual label information)
Limited scope evaluated only on EHR diagnosis and heart failure prediction; generalization to other medical domains (imaging, genomics), prediction tasks, or non-US healthcare systems remains unclear

Model complexity with multiple interacting components (MMD alignment, SAE reconstruction, orthogonal projection, domain classification) and numerous hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, λ3, ε)—limited sensitivity analysis or justification for design choices (e.g., why latent dimension 256=2d?)

Domain sensitivity annotation uses ad-hoc rank-based criterion (top-5/bottom-5) rather than principled thresholding; ∆prob=0.05 threshold for label impact appears arbitrary without systematic justification

Baseline modifications (removing self-training from RSDA/RCG, incompatibility of RCG/CST with multi-label diagnosis) raise fair comparison concerns; some improvements within ±1-2 standard errors of baselines
Three-stage training schedule lacks justification—why not joint optimization? The stopped-gradient operation on v_μ in Eq. (3) unexplained; no ablation on whether staged training is necessary

Dataset characteristics limit claims: OCHIN temporal split heavily imbalanced (2012-2021 vs 2022-2023); Figure 3 facility-based evaluation shows substantial performance degradation under severe shifts

Missing practical considerations: no computational cost analysis, failure mode discussion, or analysis of how results degrade under extreme shifts; limited discussion of when domain adaptation should NOT be used

Ethical/fairness analysis under-discussed: no investigation whether domain shifts reflect clinically meaningful differences vs artifacts, no bias analysis across patient subgroups, limited discussion of potential harms from misinterpreting domain-sensitive signals

strengths: Addresses critical gap in clinical ML: Making domain adaptation transparent and interpretable for high-stakes deployment is important and underexplored
Technically sound methodology: Dictionary-induced metric M is well-motivated; Lemma 1 and Proposition 1 provide theoretical grounding for orthogonal decomposition

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Two complementary real-world EHR datasets, multiple realistic domain shifts (spatial, temporal, facility-type), consistent improvements (9-16% relative F1 gains), thorough ablations demonstrating each component's contribution

Novel interpretability framework: Four-quadrant categorization (label impact × domain sensitivity) is intuitive and clinically actionable; external grounding protocol (RQ3) with LAD/DAD/QCE metrics rigorously validates explanations against independent anchors
Practical relevance: Facility-type adaptation (Section 4.7) demonstrates robustness under realistic shifts; interpretability enables clinician auditing rather than black-box optimization
Rigorous presentation and reproducibility: Formal mathematical exposition, extensive appendices with proofs and details, pseudocode, hyperparameters, and dataset statistics support reproducibility

Strong experimental rigor: Fair baseline comparisons, proper train/val/test splits, ablation studies convincingly demonstrate design choices, qualitative case studies (J.2) support interpretability claims
weaknesses: Theoretical gaps: Remark on 'Domain Information in z' uses informal relations (≳, ≲) with unspecified conditions rather than rigorous bounds; connection between alignment in v-space and reduced I(δ; v) lacks formal proof; weakens theoretical contribution
Limited technical novelty: Core components (SAE, orthogonal decomposition) exist in prior work; primary novelty is combining with dictionary-induced metric M, which feels somewhat incremental

Interpretation evaluation limitations: External anchors are heuristic (simple membership check for relevance); domain sensitivity uses arbitrary rank-based thresholds; human evaluation small (25 cases from 2 experts); Table 10 shows non-negligible sensitivity to label-impact threshold τ; no clinical expert validation of whether four-quadrant framework improves decision-making

Scope limited to code-level prediction: Interpretation pipeline specifically leverages ICD code structure via ablation; inapplicable to general EHR prediction (mortality, length-of-stay, lab values); narrower applicability than suggested
Modest empirical improvements: 12% relative gain on eICU diagnosis solid but not dramatic; 9% on HF trails best baseline; large gap to Oracle remains; interpretability is primary contribution

Domain classification design underexplored: Unlike standard disentanglement work, explicitly supervises z for domain classification; justified through informal information-theoretic argument but limited empirical comparison (ablation 'w/o Ldcl' insufficient)

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Introduces λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, γ, ε with limited sensitivity analysis; ε's stabilization role mathematically important but practically treated as constant; two-stage training schedule appears critical but lacks justification

Incomplete failure mode analysis: No discussion of when domain and label information are entangled; Figure 4 shows larger degradation in Mental Health/SBHC but limited analysis of why; missing adversarial examples
Limited evaluation scope: Only two prediction tasks on two similar datasets (both ICD code-based); no evaluation on non-code prediction or multimodal data; US EHR system focus limits generalization

Minimal clinical deployment discussion: Perfunctory impact statement; no fairness analysis across subgroups (age, gender, race, comorbidities); no discussion of unclear four-quadrant categorization cases; risk mitigation strategies missing
